decisions.title: Persistent Teammates vs One-Shot Subagents
decisions.description: In s04, subagents are ephemeral: spawn, do one task, return result, die. In s15, teammates are persistent entities with identity (name, role) and config files. A teammate can complete task A, then be assigned task B, carrying forward everything it learned. Persistent teammates accumulate project knowledge and don't need to re-read the same files for every task.
decisions.alternatives: One-shot subagents (s04 style) are simpler and provide perfect context isolation. But the re-learning cost is high: every new task starts from zero. A middle ground (subagents with shared memory) was considered but adds complexity without the full benefit of persistent identity.

decisions.title: Each Teammate Has Its Own Inbox File
decisions.description: Teams should not share one giant messages[] buffer. Each teammate has its own inbox file (JSONL format) and its own execution line. Coordination travels through messages between inboxes. This keeps context boundaries clean: each teammate only sees messages addressed to it, not the entire team's chatter.
decisions.alternatives: A shared message bus where everyone sees everything is simpler but creates information overload. In-memory queues don't survive process restarts. File-based inboxes provide persistence, cross-process communication, and human-debuggability.

decisions.title: The Team Lead Owns Orchestration
decisions.description: The lead builds the roster, assigns work, and watches state. Team structure is what keeps persistence understandable instead of chaotic. Without a designated lead, multiple agents trying to coordinate creates race conditions and conflicting assignments. The lead is not smarter -- it just has orchestration tools that teammates don't.
decisions.alternatives: Peer-to-peer coordination without a lead is more egalitarian but leads to coordination chaos. Distributed consensus protocols (Raft, Paxos) are correct but massively over-engineered for a local multi-agent system.
